new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable. Surface final stress arises only where the last two syllables have contracted into one (very common in verb forms: tomáwak > tomák, nimicmáka > nimicmá), i.e. stress stays on the vowel that was penultimate before contraction; a handful of locative nouns (lasiwán 'shade') have lexicalised final stress explained as old contractions. The 2015 Spanish grammar by the same author restates the rule: 'Ordinariamente, el acento en náhuatl cae en la penúltima sílaba. Cuando la penúltima sílaba se contrae con la última sílaba, el acento cae en la última y se escribe con el acento ortográfico. Ejemplo: chicahuac (fuerte, duro); chicác.' (Sischo & Erickson de Hollenbach 2015, Gramática breve del náhuatl de Michoacán, sec. 2, p.3; file).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in either source (Gordon 2023 cites Sischo 1979 among Nahuatl descriptions reporting a single stress per word).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Contracted verbals: final two syllables fuse and stress surfaces on the final syllable (tomák, úk, nimicmá; 2015: chicác, xiyén < xiyecan); (ii) a few locative words with invariable final stress, taken to be historical contractions (lasiwán 'shade'; 2015 Vocabulario: ilasehuán, amalá). The 2015 orthography marks these with a written accent, and also writes an accent on the penult when the final syllable is a bare vowel (panúa).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for the word in general (citation/isolated forms and text examples); contraction-induced final stress applies across word classes but is described as typical of verb forms. Unstressed-vowel effects (i~e, u~o fluctuation; final unstressed a raised) are keyed to this word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe the speech of Pómaro (municipio de Aquila, coastal Michoacán), the reference variety of Glottolog mich1245 / ISO ncl ('Michoacán Nahual' in SIL usage; 1979 also names Ostula, Coire and San Pedro Naranjestil as villages of the dialect). The 1765 Cortés y Zedeño Arte (Guadalajara 'mexicano falseado'), which Glottolog files under ncl as 'closest', is a different, extinct colonial Western-periphery variety and yielded no accent statement.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule (penult) and the existing statement come from exactly this chapter; the volume's only chapter on this language is Sischo's. The volume PDF itself could not be downloaded: direct download returned a not reachable by automated download challenge page, and the second attempt via web.archive.org failed to connect (automated download rc=7); the SIL landing page for 8926 was downloaded (HTTP 200) and lists the PDF link. The chapter was re-read from disk and the p.312 quote re-verified against the page image; p.358 adds the confirming 'Contraction' sentence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the penultimate syllable. When the last two syllables of a verbal contract into one (loss of k, w, y or glottal stop), the stress stays on the same vowel and so surfaces on the final syllable of the contracted form; a few locatives have invariable final stress, which Sischo attributes to old contractions.
new_statements.exceptions: Contracted verbals (and adjectives derived from verbs) with final stress (tomák, úk, nimicmá, ni-péa-k); a few locative words with invariable ultimate stress (lasiwán 'shade'), explained as historical contractions.
new_statements.identity_note: Sischo 1979 describes the Nahual of Pómaro (municipio de Aquila, coastal Michoacán), the variety the catalog entry mich1245 denotes. Guerra's Arte (1692; reprinted by Santoscoy 1900) describes the colonial Nahuatl of the Bishopric of Guadalajara 'y de parte de los de Durango y Michoacan' (western-periphery Nahuatl), attached to mich1245 by Glottolog as its closest modern relative; it is not a description of the Pómaro dialect itself and in any case contains no accent statement.
